entry.evidence: Inspired by the results of our previous study, we carefully revise the historical earthquake catalog in the Dead Sea

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML text of the published paper (nhess-22-2553-2022), checked against the PDF

steps.action: Ask whether lake-level-induced seismicity can be studied on a historical timescale despite large uncertainties in both lake-level and earthquake records.
steps.quote: Can such interactions be explored on a historical timescale when the two data types suffer from severe uncertainties

steps.action: Take over from the authors' 2018 study the hypothesis that Dead Sea water-level hikes moderate recurrence intervals on the Dead Sea Fault.
steps.quote: shown to be able to moderate the seismicity pattern at the Dead Sea Fault

steps.action: Compile published Dead Sea water-level reconstructions and anchor points (Bookman, Migowski, Stern), shift one anchor point by 40 years within its dating error, and compile the historical earthquake catalog from the literature.
steps.quote: The compilation of WL curves of the Dead Sea for the last 2 millennia from three recent publications

steps.action: Generate an ensemble of 10 million random water-level interpolations through 13 anchor points, bounded by facies constraints and smoothed by a moving average.
steps.quote: the model has generated 10 million WL curves for the last bi-millennial interval, using a uniformly distributed random number generator

steps.action: Design the test as a Pearson linear correlation between historical recurrence intervals (M > 5.5) and each interpolated water-level curve, also used to flag outliers.
steps.quote: [...] linear correlation between the RIs of the widely recorded moderate-to-large ( M > 5.5 ) historical earthquakes

steps.action: Derive from a 2D poroelastic Mohr–Coulomb strike-slip fault model (from Belferman et al. 2018) a linear dependence of simulated recurrence interval on water-level change.
steps.quote: Substitution of Eq. (1) into Eq. (3) yields a linear dependence of a simulated RI on a WL change

steps.action: Fix cohesion (C = 0.08 MPa) and reference recurrence interval (300 yr) numerically so that the model gives the 144-year average recurrence interval.
steps.quote: the cohesion, C , is not a priori known; hence it is fixed by the empirical correlation between WL and RI

steps.action: Compare all 10 million curves with the historical recurrence intervals; correlation coefficients are normally distributed with mean 0.63 and SD 0.076, and the 10 best curves are kept.
steps.quote: distributed normally around R = 0.63

steps.action: Identify three outlying historical recurrence intervals (749, 1293, 1834 CE) and re-evaluate the catalog, not the hypothesis.
steps.quote: Three outliers from the 13 RIs of the widely recorded historic earthquakes (749, 1293 and 1834 CE in Fig. 1) were identified and reevaluated

steps.action: Select the curve with the highest correlation (R = 0.912) against the revised catalog and fit the linear prediction function RI = −5442 − 14WL.
steps.quote: A curve with the highest Pearson coefficient of R = 0.912 was chosen

steps.action: Simulate a synthetic 14-event earthquake catalog and stress history from the best-fit curve with the Mohr–Coulomb model.
steps.quote: a synthetic earthquake history including 14 seismic events was simulated from the best-fit randomly interpolated WL curve

steps.action: Check that the 10 most correlated curves share the same rises, drops and maxima in water level.
steps.quote: Figure 2 shows a similar pattern of the WL change for the 10 most correlated curves.

steps.action: Compare synthetic earthquake dates with historical dates; most match, but two synthetic events (1180, 1753 CE) and three historical outliers do not.
steps.quote: The dates of these simulated synthetic earthquakes are comparable with historical earthquakes (Fig. 1e), excluding two events

steps.action: Amend the catalog to match the model: add ~1150, 1712 and 551 CE; remove 90, 112 and 659/660 CE; pair 1907 with 1927 rather than 1903; reclassify events in Tables A1–A2.
steps.quote: Summarizing the above amendments, we add to our catalog of historical events the 551, ∼ 1150 and 1712 CE earthquakes

steps.action: Admit amended (Class A) events only if they are corroborated by seismites in the northern Dead Sea cores (Ein Feshkha, Ein Gedi); this check is reported in Appendix A.
steps.quote: they are corroborated by evidence from seismites in the northern basin of the Dead Sea

steps.action: Show the water-level/recurrence-interval correlation against the literature water-level reconstructions as well as the best-fit curve.
steps.quote: The correlation between the WL and RI is noticeable for the various variants of the WL curve reconstruction (Fig. 4).

steps.action: Keep the linear relation RI = −2483 − 6.5WL for the revised catalog and best-fit curve, as consistent with the 2018 correlation.
steps.quote: This linear relationship between WL and RI underscores the previously proposed correlations between these phenomena

steps.action: Extrapolate the relation to today's −440 m level, giving a 377-year recurrence interval and a next earthquake near 2300 CE if the level stays constant.
steps.quote: we would expect the next earthquake at about ∼ 2300 CE

steps.action: Attribute the remaining misfit to unmodelled smaller or dip-slip earthquakes; argue from cited data that aftershocks are negligible and a strike-slip-only 1D model is justified.
steps.quote: the deviation might be consistent with a release of elastic energy by smaller earthquakes

steps.action: Conclude that a simple forward model gives a convincing water-level/recurrence-interval correlation and that the current lake-level decline will not trigger earthquakes by this mechanism.
steps.quote: achieves a convincing correlation between WLs and RIs of moderate-to-strong earthquakes on the Dead Sea Fault

end.claim: Over the last two millennia at the Dead Sea, earthquake recurrence intervals correlate highly and linearly with lake level (RI = −2483 − 6.5WL for the revised catalog and best-fit curve).

decisive_move.sentence: Without the 10-million-curve ensemble ranked by correlation with the (revised) recurrence intervals, there would be no best-fit lake-level scenario and no high correlation to report.

gates.evidence: No new data were acquired. The 2018 hypothesis and the model's synthetic events directed the search for and revision of catalog events, and Class A acceptance requires that 'the acceptance regularizes the relation' (§Appendix A ¶3). The correlation could have been low (the ensemble mean of 0.63 was reported before selection), but the best curve was chosen by maximum R and outliers were re-evaluated to improve the fit; no null model or significance test is reported. Nothing was fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Pearson product-moment correlation used to rank curves and flag outliers
Monte Carlo ensemble from a uniformly distributed random number generator
Historical documentary earthquake reports and catalogs (Amiran, Ambraseys, Russell)
Toponym interpretation of 'the town of Filistin' (Elad 1992; Gerber 1998)
Archaeological data justifying the 144-year average recurrence interval and event dating

novelty_claims.quote: We demonstrate for the first time a high correlation between water level changes and the recorded recurrence intervals of historical earthquakes.
We demonstrate for the first time that plausible scenarios for the lake level history can fit the record of the historical earthquake recurrence intervals

limits: No review file or discussion version was supplied, although the paper records an open discussion (started 24 March 2021) and three referees; no review sequence is coded. The order of work is inferred from the text order. No null model is reported (for example, random or shuffled catalogs), so the significance of R = 0.912, selected as the maximum of 10 million curves, is not assessed (inference: a multiple-comparison problem). Catalog revisions are partly chosen because they improve the fit (Class A criterion 1), so the correlation and the catalog are not independent (inference: circularity); seismite corroboration is the only independent constraint. Cohesion is fixed using the same correlation, and synthetic RIs vs WL fit 'R = 1' by construction. The text gives three different linear relations (Eqs. 5–7) without uncertainties. The raw data are only available on request. Sub-claims and their statuses: the best-fit lake-level curve as a plausible scenario is an estimate without stated resolution (status: none); triggering by lake-level change as the explanation is at most best_explanation, since no rival was tested; the ~2300 CE expectation is an untested extrapolation (no forecast_skill); the catalog reclassifications (Classes A and R) are best_explanation.

disagreements.target: Belferman et al. (2018) catalog inclusion of the 659/660 CE earthquake, based on Langgut et al. (2015) epicenter
disagreements.support: The rupture zone is uncertain, and the model does not support triggering shortly before the mid-8th-century lake-level low; replacing the event with 551 CE improves the fit.
disagreements.quote: However, this interpretation neglected the possibility that the rupture could have been outside the hydrological effect of the Dead Sea basin.

disagreements.target: Migowski et al. (2004) correlation of an Ein Gedi seismite with the 1656 CE earthquake
disagreements.support: Ambraseys' (2009) 1644 CE entry offers a better match; the 1656 event was strong in Tripoli and only felt in Palestine, and its seismite dating relied on deposition rates.
disagreements.quote: Given the 1644 CE entry of Ambraseys (2009), this interpretation should be revised

disagreements.target: Ambraseys (2009) reading of 'the town of Filistin' as Jerusalem for the 1644 CE event
disagreements.support: Toponym evidence (Elad 1992; Gerber 1998) suggests al-Ramla or the whole district.
disagreements.quote: While Ambraseys has interpreted it to probably be Jerusalem, it might refer to al-Ramla, the historical capital of the classical district of Filistin

disagreements.target: Russell (1985) on 551 CE destruction of Petra
disagreements.support: Newer data contradict the claim about Petra, but a failure in the Dead Sea region is kept as plausible.
disagreements.quote: Newer data contradict the assertion regarding Petra; a failure in the Dead Sea region is still plausible.

disagreements.target: Bookman et al. (2004) dating of the ~500 CE anchor point
disagreements.support: Migowski et al. (2006) and Stern (2010) place the drop later, and the shift lies within the ±45-year error.
disagreements.quote: Because this shift is within the permissible error limits ( ± 45 years), this anchor point is shifted to the left ( + 40 years).

disagreements.target: Historical catalogs listing Class R events as damaging Jerusalem (Amiran et al. 1994; Ambraseys 2009)
disagreements.support: The events are rejected after discussion of sources, locations and seismite evidence, and because the simulations do not require them.
disagreements.quote: The seven events of Class R are the debated events, rejected here after discussion.

disagreements.target: Existing explanations of earthquake triggering in the Dead Sea area (not named)
disagreements.support: Offered on the basis of the water-level/recurrence-interval correlation alone.
disagreements.quote: we offer an alternative explanation regarding the triggering of earthquakes in the area of the Dead Sea
